objectives: Decompose the eye's ~60 D total power into corneal and lenticular contributions using Gullstrand's schematic eye.
Apply the vergence equation $L' = L + P$ to locate images formed by the eye and by correcting lenses.
Differentiate myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, and presbyopia by their optical signatures and required corrections.

slides.title: The power budget of the eye — cornea, lens, and Gullstrand's schematic eye
slides.body:
The relaxed adult human eye has a total refractive power of about **+60 D**, and to use that number clinically we must know where the power comes from. The largest contribution is the **cornea**. Although the cornea is only about half a millimetre thick at its centre, it sits at the boundary between air ($n = 1.000$) and the tear film/corneal stroma ($n \approx 1.376$), and that large index step across a steeply curved front surface produces roughly **+43 D** of converging power at the anterior surface. The posterior corneal surface, between stroma ($1.376$) and aqueous humour ($1.336$), is weakly **negative**, so the net corneal power is about **+40 to +43 D** — roughly two-thirds of the eye's total.

The **crystalline lens** supplies the rest, about **+15 to +20 D** in the unaccommodated state. The lens is a remarkable biological gradient-index element: its refractive index is not uniform but rises from about $1.386$ in the cortex to about $1.406$ in the dense nucleus, which lets a relatively low-index structure achieve more power than a homogeneous lens of the same shape. Critically, the lens can **change** its power through **accommodation**, the subject of a later lesson.

The biological gradient-index design was first measured in detail by **Allvar Gullstrand** and confirmed with later **Scheimpflug** and MRI imaging; the principle that a layered index outperforms a homogeneous lens is sometimes called the **lens paradox**. To make all this calculable, the Swedish ophthalmologist **Allvar Gullstrand** (1862–1930) — who won the **1911 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** for his work on the dioptrics of the eye, presented in his appendices to **Helmholtz**'s *Handbuch der physiologischen Optik* — built the **Gullstrand schematic eye**. His detailed ("exact") model lists six refracting surfaces with measured radii and indices; his **simplified schematic eye** reduces this to a few surfaces. The full relaxed model gives a total power near **+58.6 D** with the cornea at **+43.05 D** and the lens at **+19.11 D**. Gullstrand also defined the eye's **cardinal points**: two **principal planes** (about 1.5 mm and 1.6 mm behind the cornea), two **nodal points** (about 7 mm behind the cornea), and two **focal points**.

A further idealisation, the **reduced eye** associated with **Johann Benedict Listing** (1808–1882) and later Gullstrand, collapses the whole system to a **single refracting surface** of power about **+60 D**, radius about $5.5\,\text{mm}$, with the image formed in a medium of index $1.336$ and an **axial length of about 22.2 mm**. The single nodal point sits about $7.2\,\text{mm}$ behind the cornea, which is the point we use for the simple **retinal-image-size** calculation: image height $= $ (nodal distance) $\times \tan\theta$ for an object subtending angle $\theta$. The reduced eye is accurate enough for everyday refraction and is the model we lean on for the rest of this course.

slides.title: Vergence and the vergence equation
slides.body:
Clinical optics is built almost entirely on one tool: **vergence**. The vergence $L$ of a bundle of rays at a given plane is the reciprocal of the distance (in metres) to the point the rays are converging toward or diverging from:
$$L = \frac{n}{l}$$
where $n$ is the refractive index of the medium and $l$ is the signed distance. By the **sign convention** (light travels left to right, distances measured from the lens), **diverging** light has **negative** vergence and **converging** light has **positive** vergence. Vergence, like power, is measured in **diopters**.

The central relationship is the **vergence equation** (sometimes called the **fundamental paraxial equation** or **Gauss's lens-step equation**, after **Carl Friedrich Gauss** (1777–1855), whose 1841 *Dioptrische Untersuchungen* founded the paraxial theory of cardinal points):
$$L' = L + P$$
where $L$ is the **incident** (object) vergence, $P$ is the **surface or lens power**, and $L'$ is the **emergent** (image) vergence. In words: *a lens changes vergence by exactly its power*. Once you know $L'$, the image location follows from $l' = n'/L'$.

A worked example anchors the idea. Suppose an object sits $50\,\text{cm}$ ($0.5\,\text{m}$) in front of a $+5.00\,\text{D}$ thin lens in air. The incident vergence is
$$L = \frac{1}{-0.5\,\text{m}} = -2.00\,\text{D}$$
(negative because the object is to the left, so the light diverges as it reaches the lens). Then
$$L' = L + P = -2.00 + 5.00 = +3.00\,\text{D},$$
and the image distance is $l' = 1/(+3.00) = +0.333\,\text{m}$, a real image $33.3\,\text{cm}$ behind the lens. The positive sign confirms the image is real and on the far side.

Vergence makes **spectacle correction** transparent. A distant object sends **parallel light** ($L = 0$) to the eye. An emmetropic eye supplies $+60\,\text{D}$ and focuses it on the retina ($L' = +60\,\text{D}$ inside the $n = 1.336$ vitreous). A myopic eye supplies *too much* power, so its image vergence overshoots. The correcting minus lens reduces the vergence reaching the eye by exactly the amount needed. Because lenses in contact add ($P_{\text{total}} = P_1 + P_2$), the optometrist can think of the spectacle and the eye as one combined system. Vergence also explains **vertex distance** corrections: when a lens is moved, the vergence arriving at the eye changes, so a strong lens worn closer (a contact lens) needs a slightly different power than the same correction worn at the spectacle plane — a calculation we formalise with the **effective power** formula $P_{\text{eff}} = P / (1 - dP)$ where $d$ is the shift in metres.

slides.title: The four classical refractive errors and the near and far points
slides.body:
Donders' taxonomy of refractive error, refined over the following century, recognises four conditions an optometrist corrects daily. Each has a distinct optical signature.

**Myopia** (nearsightedness): the eye is **too powerful for its axial length**, so parallel rays focus in front of the retina. The **far point** is at a finite distance in front of the eye; objects beyond it blur. Correction is a **diverging (minus) lens** whose secondary focal point coincides with the far point. Subtypes include **axial myopia** (long eye) and **refractive (curvature/index) myopia** (steep cornea or a swollen, high-index lens, as in nuclear cataract or hyperglycaemia).

**Hyperopia** (farsightedness): the eye is **too weak for its length**, so parallel rays focus behind the retina; the far point is **virtual** (behind the eye). The correction is a **converging (plus) lens**. Young hyperopes often hide the error by accommodating (latent hyperopia), which is why **cycloplegic refraction** is used in children.

**Astigmatism**: the refracting surfaces — usually the cornea — are not spherical but **toric**, with different curvatures in different meridians, so there is no single focus but two focal lines separated by the **interval of Sturm** (after the conoid of **Charles-François Sturm**, 1803–1855). The **circle of least confusion** lies between the two line foci. Astigmatism was first described in the human eye by **Thomas Young** in **1801** and clinically corrected with a cylindrical lens by **George Biddell Airy** (1801–1892), the future Astronomer Royal, in **1825** for his own eye. Astigmatism is corrected with a **cylindrical (or sphero-cylindrical) lens** specified by power and **axis**. **With-the-rule** astigmatism has the steepest corneal meridian near vertical; **against-the-rule** near horizontal.

**Presbyopia**: not a focusing error of distance vision but the **age-related loss of accommodation** as the crystalline lens stiffens. Beginning around the mid-40s, the **amplitude of accommodation** falls below the demand of reading distance, and a **plus 'add'** is required for near work (reading glasses, bifocals, or progressive lenses).

Two landmarks bracket the eye's range of clear vision. The **far point** (*punctum remotum*) is the most distant point seen clearly with accommodation **relaxed**; the **near point** (*punctum proximum*) is the closest point seen clearly with accommodation **maximal**. The dioptric difference between them is the **amplitude of accommodation**:
$$A = \frac{1}{\text{near point (m)}} - \frac{1}{\text{far point (m)}}.$$
For a young emmetrope with a near point of $10\,\text{cm}$ and a far point at infinity, $A = 1/0.10 - 0 = +10\,\text{D}$. **Donders** and **Edward Landolt** (1846–1926) tabulated how this amplitude declines with age — roughly $15\,\text{D}$ at age 10 falling to about $1\,\text{D}$ by age 60 — the empirical basis of the presbyopic 'add' that we calculate in the binocular-vision lesson.

question.question: An object sits $0.25\,\text{m}$ in front of a thin lens of power $+8.00\,\text{D}$ in air. Using the vergence equation $L' = L + P$, find the emergent vergence $L'$ in diopters.
question.hint: Incident vergence $L = 1/(-0.25) = -4.00\,\text{D}$; then add the lens power.

question.question: In Gullstrand's relaxed schematic eye, which statement about the eye's power budget is most accurate?
options: The crystalline lens provides about two-thirds of the eye's power and the cornea about one-third.
The cornea provides about +43 D and the lens about +19 D, summing to roughly +59 D total.
The cornea is optically neutral; essentially all refraction occurs at the crystalline lens.
The posterior corneal surface is the strongest converging surface in the eye.
question.explanation: Gullstrand's relaxed schematic eye assigns about +43 D to the cornea and about +19 D to the crystalline lens, for a total near +58.6–59 D. The cornea dominates because the largest index step in the eye occurs at the air–tear–cornea interface across a steeply curved surface; it supplies roughly two-thirds of the total power, not one-third (so option A is reversed). The cornea is far from neutral (option C), and the posterior corneal surface is actually weakly negative because it goes from higher-index stroma (1.376) to lower-index aqueous (1.336), so it is not the strongest converging surface (option D).

hints: The cornea, not the lens, carries most of the power.
Think roughly +43 D cornea plus ~+19 D lens.
slides.workedSolution: In Gullstrand's relaxed (simplified) schematic eye the cornea contributes about +43 D and the unaccommodated crystalline lens about +19 D, giving a total near +58.6 D, conventionally rounded to ~60 D. The cornea dominates (about two-thirds) because the biggest refractive-index jump in the eye is at the air/tear/cornea interface. Option B captures both the split and the sum correctly.

question.question: A young patient has a far point at optical infinity and a near point at $12.5\,\text{cm}$. Compute the amplitude of accommodation in diopters using $A = 1/\text{near} - 1/\text{far}$ (distances in metres).

A 48-year-old emmetrope reports that distance vision is perfect but small print at reading distance has become blurry and tiring over the past two years. What is the optical explanation and the appropriate correction?
options: Axial myopia; prescribe a minus distance lens.
Astigmatism from a toric cornea; prescribe a cylindrical lens.
Presbyopia from age-related loss of accommodative amplitude; prescribe a plus reading add.
Latent hyperopia unmasked by fatigue; prescribe a strong minus add for near.
question.explanation: An emmetrope with crisp distance vision has no spherical distance error, so options A and D (which alter distance correction or prescribe minus for near) are wrong. The age (~48) and the symptom pattern — distance fine, near increasingly blurred and tiring — are the textbook presentation of presbyopia: the crystalline lens has stiffened and the amplitude of accommodation has fallen below the dioptric demand of reading distance. The remedy is a plus reading 'add' (reading glasses, bifocals, or a progressive addition lens) that supplies the missing near power. Astigmatism (option B) would blur both distance and near and is unrelated to the age-linked near-only complaint.

hints: Distance vision is perfect, so the distance sphere is fine.
Late 40s plus near-only blur points to a loss of accommodation.
slides.workedSolution: The patient is emmetropic at distance, so there is no distance refractive error to correct. The hallmark of presbyopia is the gradual decline of accommodative amplitude with age (about +10 D at 25 falling toward +1 D by 60). By the late 40s the amplitude can no longer meet the ~2.5–3 D demand of a 33–40 cm reading distance, so near print blurs and the eyes tire. The correct management is a plus near add, hence option C.

question.question: Deciding between contact-lens and spectacle power for a high myope
question.prompt: A high myope has a well-tolerated spectacle prescription of $-10.00\,\text{D}$ worn at a vertex distance of $14\,\text{mm}$, and now wants contact lenses that sit on the cornea. Explain, using the concept of vergence and the effective-power relationship $P_{\text{eff}} = P/(1 - dP)$, why the contact-lens power should differ from the spectacle power, in which direction the power must change for a minus lens moved closer to the eye, and roughly by how much. Then state why this vertex-distance effect is clinically negligible for a $-1.00\,\text{D}$ patient but important here.
